summary: Describes a model for operational statistics in the Internet, for use by tools that collect and report on network performance and usage. It is informational and defines a model and protocol, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1857 describes a shared way to measure a network. It names a small set of counters worth collecting, says how often to read them, defines a plain-text file format for storing them, and describes the reports that can be made from the data. The aim is that statistics from different network operation centres can be compared, and shared for planning.

questions: what is a model for operational statistics
how to measure internet operational statistics

subtitle: A common recipe for which network counters to collect, how often, how to store them and how to report them.

tldr.problem: Network operators collected counters about traffic and reliability, but each network measured and presented them differently, so data from different sites could not be compared, and there was no agreement on which counters mattered.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a model in three parts: a minimal set of twelve counters from the Internet Standard MIB, a common plain-text file format with device, label and data sections, and a set of report formats, with recommended polling and aggregation periods for each.
tldr.outcome: Data collected at one site could be stored in the common format and read by common presentation tools, which the memo hopes would let network operation centres share statistics and plan together.

facts.label: Retention scheme
facts.value: 1 minute data 1 day, 15 minute 1 week, 1 hour 1 month, 1 day 1 year

today: RFC 1857 is an Informational memo published in October 1995, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It revises RFC 1404 with a model for collecting, storing and reporting operational statistics, and points to RFC 1856 for a client/server way of exchanging them.

sections.title: Why a Common Model
sections.content:
Many network administrations commonly collect and archive network management metrics that indicate network utilization, growth and reliability. The primary goals of this activity are to facilitate near-term problem isolation and longer-term network planning within the organisation, and there is the broader goal of cooperative problem isolation and network planning among network administrations.

The obstacle is that a variety of network management tools exist for the collection and presentation of metrics, but different kinds of measurement and presentation technique make it difficult to compare data among networks. There is also no general agreement on what metrics should be regularly collected or how they should be displayed.

The memo therefore argues for an agreed-upon model: a minimal set of common network management metrics, tools for collecting them, a common interchange format that lets common presentation tools use the data, and common presentation formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Network operators already collect counters about how much traffic their network carries, but each network measures and reports differently, so the numbers cannot be compared. The memo proposes a shared set of counters, a shared way to store them and a shared way to present them.

sections.title: The Model and Its Three Areas
sections.content:
The model defines three areas of interest. First, the definition of a minimal set of metrics to be gathered. Second, the definition of a format for storing collected statistical data. Third, the definition of methods and formats for generating reports.

Within the model, collection tools collect and store data to be retrieved later in a given format by presentation tools that display the data in a predefined way. The memo notes that old tools in use could be retrofitted into the new paradigm by providing conversion filters between old and new tools, and it advocates the development of freely redistributable software for participating network operation centres. One basic idea of the model is that statistical data stored in one place could be retrieved and displayed in some other place.

The memo also flags the problems of sharing data. There are legal, ethical and political concerns, and people, in particular network service providers, are concerned about showing data that may make one of their networks look bad. For this reason there is a need to assure the integrity, conformity and confidentiality of the shared data. To be useful, the same data should be collected from all involved sites, and it should be collected at the same interval.
sections.plainLanguage: The model has three parts: choose a small set of counters to gather, define a file format to store them in, and define the reports to produce from them. Data collected at one site can then be stored in the common format and read by a presentation tool elsewhere.

sections.title: Categories of Metrics and the Recommended Set
sections.content:
Metrics fall into four categories by what they measure. Utilization metrics describe aspects of the total traffic being forwarded through the network, with candidates such as total input and output packets and octets, peak metrics, and per protocol and per application metrics. Performance metrics relate to quality of service issues such as delays and congestion, for example round trip time metrics on different protocol layers, collisions on a bus network, ICMP Source Quench messages and packets dropped. Availability metrics gauge long term accessibility on different protocol layers, such as line availability as percentage uptime, route availability and application availability. Stability metrics describe short-term fluctuations that degrade the service level, such as fast line status transitions, route flapping, the number of routes per interface and next hop count stability.

The metrics are also grouped by how hard they are to retrieve. Some are already variables in the Internet Standard MIB and are easy to retrieve. Some may be retrievable because they are part of a vendor's private enterprise MIB. Some need high resolution polling, which is hard because of the network load it creates. Some are in no known MIB, so they cannot be retrieved using SNMP but could be included in one. Some, such as delays on different protocol layers, application layer availability and peak behaviour metrics, cannot be retrieved with SNMP at all.

The recommended minimal set is drawn from the Internet Standard MIB, since general retrievability is equated with presence there. For each interface: ifInOctets, ifOutOctets, ifInUcastPkts, ifOutUcastPkts, ifInNUcastPkts, ifOutNUcastPkts, ifInDiscards, ifOutDiscards and ifOperStatus. For each node: ipForwDatagrams, ipInDiscards and sysUpTime. The memo notes that many metrics regarded as important are not currently defined in the standard MIB, and that the decisions should be revisited if that changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Counters are sorted two ways: by what they tell you, such as how busy the network is or how reliable it is, and by how hard they are to fetch. The recommended list is the twelve counters that a standard SNMP tool can already read everywhere.

sections.title: Polling Frequencies and Aggregation
sections.content:
The purpose of polling at specified intervals is to gather statistics to serve as a basis for trend and capacity planning, and from the operational data it should be possible to derive engineering and management data. The memo notes that all polling and retention values it gives are recommendations and are not mandatory.

To be able to detect peak behaviour, it recommends a period of 1 minute, 60 seconds, at a maximum for gathering traffic data. The variables collected at this frequency are, for each interface, ifInOctets, ifOutOctets, ifInUcastPkts and ifOutUcastPkts. If that is not possible, an exact multiple of 60 seconds is recommended. The remaining recommended variables, the five per interface and the three per node, can be collected at a lower polling rate; no rate is specified, but the period chosen should again be an exact multiple of 60 seconds.

Raw data is pre-processed before storage to avoid redundancy. The variables sysUpTime and ifOperStatus make it possible not to store data collected from links and nodes where no traffic has been transmitted for some period of time. Data is also decoupled from the raw interface being polled, so that a change of interface in a gateway for a given link is not visible in the result. Aggregation replaces the values on a number of time intervals with some function of the values over the union of those intervals, and the memo notes that aggregation reduces the amount of data but also reduces the available information. The function used is either the arithmetic mean or the maximum, depending on whether the average or the peak value of a variable is wanted. The suggested periods are: over a 24 hour period aggregate to 15 minutes, over a 1 month period to 1 hour, over a 1 year period to 1 day.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo asks for the busiest traffic counters to be read once a minute, and the rest less often. Readings are then combined over longer periods to keep the file small, and the combination is either an average or the maximum, depending on whether the report needs the average load or the worst one.

sections.title: The Statistical Data File Format
sections.content:
The storage format is designed to minimize redundant information and thus storage requirements, and to provide complete, self-contained, portable files rather than to describe a full database for storing them. If a client server based model for retrieving remote statistical data were developed later, the format could serve as the transmission protocol. All white space is ignored, and all text from a # symbol to the end of the line is ignored.

A file is a sequence of sections: device sections, label sections and data sections. A data file must contain at least one device section and at least one label section, at least one data section must be associated with each label section, and a device section must precede any data section which uses tags defined within it. A label section gives the start and stop times for its data section or sections and a list of the tags they contain; the times are in UTC, written as year, month, day, hour, minute and second. A device section names the network, the router, the link, the bandwidth in bits per second, the protocol type, which may be IP, DECNET, X.25, CLNS, IPX or AppleTalk, the numeric address of the interface and the time zone, and may carry a tag table listing the variables polled with their initial polling period and aggregation period in seconds.

A data section holds one data field for each separate poll. Each field begins with the timestamp, then the tag, then a poll delta giving the period in seconds since the previous poll, then the values: counter variables are stored as delta values and non-counter values, such as the interface status, as absolute values. Comma, semicolon or colon may be used as the field separator, and parentheses, brackets or braces may enclose the tag-name, tag-table and delta-value lists.

The memo estimates the storage needed for one year. With the maximum polling intensity used for all 12 recommended variables, eight bytes for each variable and no fractional timestamps, keeping one minute of data for a day, 15 minute aggregation for a week, 1 hour aggregation for a month and 1 day aggregation for a year gives a grand total of 775 kB.
sections.plainLanguage: The file has three kinds of section. A device section describes the link the data came from, a label section gives the time range and the names of the counters, and a data section holds one line per poll with the changes in each counter. The file is plain text, and a year of data at the recommended rates is estimated at 775 kB.

sections.title: Report Formats and Further Work
sections.content:
The memo suggests several report types. Daily reports give the instantaneous overviews needed in the daily operations of a network, weekly reports give information about medium-term changes in network behaviour which could serve as input to the medium-term engineering approach, and monthly and yearly reports show long-term tendencies. Each should report offered load, meaning total traffic at external interfaces, segmented by customer and by protocol or application, and resource utilization for links and routers.

Offered load by link covers input and output octets and packets per external interface, which could be visualised as a bar chart of the totals for the four metric categories on an hourly, daily, monthly or yearly basis. Offered load by customer covers the same four categories per customer, sorted in decreasing order, with a cumulative plot of the percentage of traffic offered to the top n customers; the definition of a customer has to be made locally at the site gathering the statistics.

Resource utilization reporting uses peak behaviour. The polling interval must be small enough to be significant with respect to variations in human activity, since that activity drives variations in network loading, but there is no need to make it smaller than an interval over which excessive delay would notably affect productivity. For this reason 30 minutes is given as a good estimate of the time people remain in one activity, and tracking 30 minute variations means sampling twice as frequently, every 15 minutes. A possible format combines the average and the maximum for a period on the same diagram, in the manner of peak meters on audio equipment, so that line utilization and bottlenecks due to temporary high loads can be detected. A second option is a histogram of the samples showing the relative frequency of load against the load itself.

For further development the memo suggests a client/server architecture, in which each network operation centre installs a server that provides locally collected information in a variety of forms, and a client uses a query language to ask for the network object, interface, metrics and time period it wants, with the server transmitting the data over TCP; this is discussed further by Henry Clark in RFC 1856. It also suggests specifying a subtree of the Internet Standard MIB for operational statistics, and a way to gather the per application and per protocol statistics that tools such as the NSF NNStat collect today.
sections.plainLanguage: The reports come in daily, weekly, monthly and yearly versions, all built from offered load and resource utilization. Utilization is reported as a peak, because a link that is busy for a quarter of an hour is what causes trouble.
